The Red River of the South. Distinct from the Red River flowing into Hudson Bay, this Red River flows approximately one thousand three hundred miles from the Texas Panhandle eastward through Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Louisiana to its confluence with the Mississippi River. It forms portions of state boundaries and drains a significant portion of the south-central United States. The river originates in the Texas Panhandle and flows eastward through semi-arid to subtropical regions before meeting the Mississippi in Louisiana. It was named for the reddish clay and sediment that colors its waters, particularly visible during high-water periods. The Red River forms the boundary between Texas and Oklahoma for much of its course and between Texas and Arkansas in another section. The river valley was located in a region historically contested between the United States and the Spanish colonial empire, with the river serving as a boundary in various treaties. It receives major tributaries including the Washita River and the Ouachita River in Louisiana, adding to its flow. The river valley was crucial to early American frontier expansion during the nineteenth century, though this expansion came at the cost of Native American displacement and tragic removal. The Red River is subject to significant seasonal variation, with spring flooding common. Generally smaller and more erratic than the Mississippi or Missouri, it nonetheless remains an important feature of the southern landscape and the boundary between the states it separates.
